passage: Both Nitrogen and Magnesium are phloem-mobile elements. When soil supply is deficient or root uptake is compromised, the plant translocates these mobile nutrients from mature basal foliage to the active meristem. Consequently, symptoms appear first on older, lower leaves. True Nitrogen deficiency manifests as generalized, uniform pale chlorosis across the blade, whereas Magnesium deficiency produces distinct interveinal chlorosis with green secondary and tertiary venation.

topic: Root Zone Anoxia & Impaired Active Transport
passage: Prolonged saturation of the pore space restricts oxygen diffusion (diffusion coefficient of O2 in water is ~10,000 times lower than in air). Root cells shift to anaerobic fermentation, causing ATP depletion. Because root uptake of mobile nutrients (nitrate, magnesium, potassium) requires active H+-ATPase proton pumping, anoxic roots fail to absorb nutrients even when abundant in soil, inducing pseudo-deficiency symptoms (leaf yellowing) accompanied by epinasty or wilt.

Soil-borne vascular fungi penetrate through lateral root emergence zones and colonize xylem vessels, inducing tyloses that physically obstruct water and mineral translocation. A hallmark diagnostic criterion distinguishing vascular wilt from abiotic nutrient deficits is sectorial asymmetry: yellowing frequently begins on one side of a compound leaf or along a single lower branch before spreading systemically.

Sudden transitions from overcast, moisture-saturated weather to intense solar irradiance exceed the photoprotective capacity of photosystem II (PSII). Reactive oxygen species (ROS) degrade chlorophyll pigments, causing photobleaching and marginal scorching specifically on sun-exposed upper surfaces, leaving shaded lower leaves unblemished.

topic: Bacterial Leaf Blight vs Physiological Bronzing in Indian Paddy
passage: In waterlogged Indian rice basins across Punjab, Andhra Pradesh, and West Bengal, growers often mistake early Bacterial Leaf Blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae) for nutrient deficiency. BLB exhibits distinctive wavy marginal water-soaked lesions that turn straw-yellow, exudating milky bacterial ooze during humid mornings. In contrast, Zinc deficiency (Khaira disease) manifests 2-3 weeks after transplanting as reddish-brown pigmentation or bronzing on older leaves without bacterial bacterial streaming.
scientificKey: Bacterial Leaf Blight (Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzae)

topic: Cotton Wilt Complex in Vertisols (Black Cotton Soils)
passage: In Indian black cotton soils (Deccan Plateau / Maharashtra / Gujarat), high montmorillonite clay content causes severe shrink-swell behavior. Waterlogging during heavy monsoon spells causes root asphyxiation, predisposing cotton to Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum and Rhizoctonia bataticola (dry root rot). Scraping the lower stem cambium ring reveals deep chocolate-brown vascular xylem discoloration, distinguishing fungal wilt from temporary parawilt (anoxia-induced foliar drooping).

topic: Pigeonpea & Chickpea Wilt in Rainfed Indian Agronomy
passage: In semi-arid pulse tracts (Madhya Pradesh, Karnataka), Fusarium udum (pigeonpea) and Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. ciceris (chickpea) cause devastating losses. Unlike general drought stress where all plants wilt simultaneously across an entire field parcel, Fusarium wilt strikes in patches or individual plants along the furrow. Splitting the taproot longitudinally reveals distinct dark purple or brown xylem vascular bands running upwards from the root collar.

topic: Lime-Induced Iron Chlorosis in Calcareous Semi-Arid Soils
passage: In calcareous soils containing high free calcium carbonate (CaCO3) with pH > 7.8 (common in western and central India), iron (Fe2+) is precipitated as insoluble ferric hydroxides. Because Iron is phloem-immobile, deficiency symptoms first manifest as intense ivory-white or bright lemon-yellow chlorosis on the youngest emerging terminal shoots and leaflets, with green veins sharply preserved. Standard soil iron application fails; foliar chelated iron (Fe-EDDHA) is required.
